findings.title: Adjusting for total energy decides what a nutrient's coefficient means.
findings.detail: `kcal` is total energy. `protein`, `sugar`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat` and 2 more carry energy, and each correlates 0.67 to 0.88 with `kcal`.
findings.why_it_matters: Adjusting for total energy makes a nutrient's coefficient a substitution: more of it in place of other energy at the same total. Leaving energy out, or partitioning it, asks about adding energy instead. The two answer different questions (Tomova et al. 2022), so which to ask is the study's choice and the method follows from it. For prediction, models that keep total energy predict alike.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

findings.summary: `fat_total` correlates 0.88 with `kcal` across all `21,849` rows: nutrient effects are tangled with total energy.

findings.title: Adjusting for total energy decides what a nutrient's coefficient means.

assumptions.label: No unmeasured confounding
assumptions.statement: Given the adjustment set, `sugar` is as good as randomly assigned.
assumptions.diagnostic: Adjusted for `kcal`, `protein`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat` and 5 more, as the disjunctive cause criterion's answers decided. No data can confirm this: a sensitivity analysis to an unmeasured confounder is required beside the estimate.
assumptions.source: Hernán & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If, §3

assumptions.label: Positivity
assumptions.statement: `sugar` still varies at every level of the covariates.
assumptions.diagnostic: The covariates explain 76% of `sugar`'s variance; what is left has a standard deviation of 39.17.
assumptions.source: Hernán & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If, §3

assumptions.label: Consistency
assumptions.statement: `sugar` is one well-defined intervention, so the outcome observed under it is the outcome it would cause.
assumptions.diagnostic: `sugar` is compared per unit; as a substitution at fixed total energy, which names the intervention (Tomova et al. 2022).
assumptions.source: Hernán & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If, §3

assumptions.label: Time ordering
assumptions.statement: The covariates precede `sugar`, and `sugar` precedes the outcome.
assumptions.diagnostic: `weight`, `height`, `bmi` and `waist` are of unknown timing and stay out of the primary set (the declared with-and-without pair); the rest were answered as set before the exposure.
assumptions.source: Hernán & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If, §3

steps.label: Ordinary least squares
steps.detail: Fits the straight-line effect of every column. The coefficient table uses every analyzed row; intervals use HC3 robust standard errors, or CR2 cluster-robust ones when a unit's rows repeat, or Taylor linearization over a survey design.

base.estimand: More of each nutrient with total energy held fixed: with protein, carbohydrate and fat all in the model, each coefficient is a substitution in place of the energy sources not in the model: alcohol, other. It is not a swap for the average of all other sources (NUTRITION_PACK §05a: name the omitted component). carb sits beside its own parts sugar, so its coefficient is the remaining carbohydrate (holding sugar fixed): the carbohydrate in none of them, not total carbohydrate. fat_total sits beside its own parts fat_sat, fat_mon and fat_poly, so its coefficient is the remaining fat (holding fat_sat, fat_mon, fat_poly fixed): the fat in none of them, not total fat.
warnings: sugar is a part of carb: carb's coefficient is the remainder (holding sugar fixed), not total carb; leave it out to estimate the total. A substitution through carb moves it in proportion, and never pairs carb with its own part.

fat_sat, fat_mon, fat_poly are parts of fat_total: fat_total's coefficient is the remainder (holding fat_sat, fat_mon, fat_poly fixed), not total fat_total; leave them out to estimate the total. A substitution through fat_total moves them in proportion, and never pairs fat_total with its own part.

robustness.interval_note: The robustness value for the 95% interval and the benchmarks' adjusted intervals rest on the classical least-squares standard error (0.00592), as sensemakr computes them; the interval reported uses HC3 standard errors, 0.00651, so they are not reported: they would describe an interval that is not the one shown.

sensitivity.reading: An unmeasured confounder would need a partial R² of 2.3% with both `sugar` and `glucose`, beyond the measured covariates, to bring the estimate to zero (Cinelli & Hazlett 2020, J R Stat Soc B 82:39); one as strong as `carb` would move it to 0.03358. The robustness value for the 95% interval and the benchmarks' adjusted intervals rest on the classical least-squares standard error (0.00592), as sensemakr computes them; the interval reported uses HC3 standard errors, 0.00651, so they are not reported: they would describe an interval that is not the one shown. E-value for the estimate: 1.02, and for the confidence limit nearer the null 1.01 (VanderWeele & Ding 2017, Ann Intern Med 167:268); an E-value is read against the confounders one can name, never as a pass or a fail.

base.methods: The estimate of `sugar` is reported across a declared sequence of models fit on all 21,849 analyzed rows: unadjusted; Model 2, the primary, adjusted for `kcal`, `protein`, `carb`, `fat_total`, `fat_sat`, `fat_mon`, `fat_poly` and 3 more; Model 3, further adjusted for `weight`, `height`, `bmi` and `waist`, possible mediators, so not a total effect. Only the exposure's estimates are shown as effects; every other coefficient is listed apart as an adjustment term, not an effect estimate (Westreich & Greenland 2013, Am J Epidemiol 177:292). Influence was checked by Cook's distance against the median of F(19, 21,830) (Cook 1977, Technometrics 19:15): 0 rows above it. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is reported by the Cinelli–Hazlett robustness value (each adjusted covariate a named benchmark; its form for the 95% interval, and the benchmarks' intervals, are not reported, as they assume classical standard errors and the intervals reported are HC3) and by the E-value for the estimate and for the confidence limit nearer the null, never as a pass or a fail.

base.estimand: The average change in predicted glucose when k kcal move from sugar to protein, their parts or totals moving with them and every other input, total energy included, left as it was.
base.note: Total energy was held fixed by assumption: intake can rise or fall, so keeping the total constant is a modeling choice, not a property of the data. Rows whose shifted sugar or protein would leave the observed range or go negative, or whose share of energy from either (of kcal) would leave the range of that share observed, are left out at that k, and the curve stops at the first k where fewer than 50% of rows remain; that 50% floor (min_support) is a practitioner convention, not a sourced threshold. The curve stopped at k = 400 kcal, where 48% of rows remained on support. Each k averages over its own on-support rows, so the rows behind the curve change with k; the fixed-population curve averages over the same 3,220 rows, those on support at every k up to 300 kcal. On every row, sugar is part of carb, so carb moved with it by the same amount while its other parts held. The model holds protein, carb and fat_total; alcohol and other energy make up the rest of total energy, 1% of it on average, and more than 10% on 2,021 of 21,849 rows. Total energy carries them as one composite, so the curve carries their confounding (Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant 2022: "wherever ≥2 components are involved in the substitution, there is scope for composite variable bias unless the individual effects are estimated"); add the remaining sources to the model to remove it. sugar moves at 4 kcal per unit, recorded in g: carbohydrate at 4 kcal/g. protein is read in grams by its values (the Atwater identity holds with total energy), at 4 kcal per gram.
